title: I Mapped All 189,495 Steam Games to Find What’s Missing
author: re-skob
selftext: Created this IdeaPlotter video. Thought it was interesting. Novel does not mean good. The best games are within the big groupings and have a clear identity, not just "never made before" which is probably one of the worst metrics for creating a successful game. The whole concept of "AI can't make anything new" is silly, as making something new isn't actually a valuable metric that anybody really makes decisions around and people in general don't "make anything new." Every game ever made can be reduced down to "It's like this but with that" all the way back to the first video game Pong that's "like ping-pong but on a computer." And good games aren't just a steam page description and a set of tags, they're the thousands of decisions that the developer has to make during the course of production.

comments.author: MikeSemicolonD
comments.body:
So basically a system that devises what it 'thinks' is an original idea by trying to deviate from current games related to it. 

Cool on the surface of it, but how exactly does it determine closeness to an idea beyond just what the description, title and genres states it is? Using review count as a statistic too is very odd.. This system doesn't actually play the games, hears the sounds, and understands the story and game pace in a way that it's able to determine 'closeness'. 

You basically made a recommendation system that recommends ideas that are designed to be different from it's neighbors.

Recommendation systems historically are always really bad at recommending because it doesn't take into account the smaller minute details of what users actually liked. The only way around that is a survey for your target market and mostly no one's going to do that.. 

What that means is most of these ideas end up as the equivalent of word salad for the sake of just being different. Cradle Gambit for example does not sound fun, it sounds like a weird monopoly 'racing?' game about getting cribs and blankets.. Yet your system says '0.60' (slightly clipping over text there) similar to real game then show a stat of 98.7% "of Steam games have a closer twin" and mention 'Board Wars - Trick Or Treat'. 

If those stats are meant to give a hint on uniqueness these stats are literally meaningless because how you're measuring it is wildly off.. If you made Cradle Gambit it'll probably look and play nearly like 'Board Wars - Trick Or Treat'. But oh the system said it was unique because you're getting cradles and blankets in Rome..

comments.author: kevin_whitley
comments.body:
IMO: This effort should be towards mapping the vector space for better recommendation engines (games, books, whatever)

Today, it seems like's rec. engines are dumb AF, based almost purely on tags.  Like 1 survival game?  Here, you might like these other 1000 with the same "survival crafting" tag.

Instead, it should be able to look at all our reviews, thumbs up/thumbs downs, returns, hours played, etc and find the fingerprint that matches that.  In theory there's another gamer out there with a similar pattern, so looking at what THEY have played that we haven't is a way better idea than just tag-matching.

comments.author: kaliffen79
comments.body:
while this is very interesting and a worthwhile approach, I find two fundamental flaws with this method.

1) judging a game from its marketing material, is like judging food from the picture they show at cetrain resturants/bistros.

1a) some warped form of this argument also applies to reviews.

2) The concept of "game idea" its not really well defined.  (Not here, nor anywhere in the industry).   
\- It it the lore and world?  its it the mechanics and player experience?  Is it everything?  can multiple implementations realize the same idea differently?  does that change the idea?

2a) the closest I have come to what an game idea is, "its the pitch that sells the idea to someone"  
it is never the game itself, and ideas always change when realized.

I am not trying to rain on your parade, Just offering my thoughts. This is very cool.

replies.author: re-skob

I'm glad people are finding this interesting and having good discussions on how they approach making something good

replies.author: kaliffen79
replies.body:
Interesting.  The question then becomes, what really defines something being new then.  
If I have a boat, that I have sailed with for many years called "Anna", how many parts can I then replace before I must rename her?

this is an age old question, and the most reasonable answer, I find, is that Identity is purely invented.  
Is is a human projection mechanism.  This does not make it less strong or less worth to pursue.  
From this angle I might push back slightly on the notion that "new" can be defined as a re-mix of something already existing.  
This might be what humans excel at.  Pulling something from the aether, that actually was not materialized before.  
This is not a remix, but an organic unique impression.

While this carries some weight, I can also see the angle,  
were covering unexplored space, means exploration, ie. uncovering new things.  
And many things today considered "new" ARE just remixes.

My point here is just, that these things mostly lie on a gray line and, that the devil is in the detail.  
Quality is not the same as being functional.  Price of software lines may have decreased significantly, but I'm still not convinced that real quality can be obtained, in any other, than the hard way.

I am a bit off topic here :)
